Ray Conniff

The fall of 1997 was an eventful time for Ray Conniff as he celebrated his 81st birthday and the release of his 100th album, “I Love Movies.” Ray has become a legend in the music world as an arranger, producer and creator of “a sound.”

His distinctive blend of big band, orchestral and vocal scoring captured the ears of American listeners in the late 1950s and became a familiar sound on radio and home stereos. He started as a trombonist and arranger in the active years of swing, writing for Bunny Berigan, Artie Shaw, Benny Goodman and other big band leaders. His association with Mitch Miller at Columbia Records led to his first records under his own name, and he now places on the top ten all-time album sellers. His six decade career in music is testament to an acute business sense and the ability to create scores which satisfy his love of arranging while honoring the melody of the song.
Ray currently lives in Los Angeles, and was interviewed in San Diego, California on February 14, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

We are filming in San Diego for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. And I am honored to have Mr. Ray Conniff with me — trombonist and arranger and composer. And I want to tell you that when I grew up, in the 50s, I lived outside Rochester, New York, and it was kind of a typical suburban home, and in my house, my parents played Glenn Miller and a little Basie, and a lot of Ray Conniff. So it’s a real pleasure for me to be talking with you today, because your sound is something that was present a lot as I grew up. I think probably it’s a pretty huge compliment to have people refer to “a sound,” you know, like “well what we need is that Ray Conniff sound.” And it’s been a long road, but would you do it all again?
Would I what?
Would you do it all again?

[coughs] pardon me. I hope there won’t be too much of that going on. I’ve got one of these California flu bugs or something. Oh, sure, you know, as we live life at the time, when we’re doing, like now what we’re doing, we think we’re doing the right thing for now. And I guess if you went back and looked at every now, you thought you were doing — I can see times when I probably could have done something a little differently, but I think on the whole, yeah, I’ve been very fortunate. Well the main thing I guess I’ve been fortunate about is that there aren’t a lot of men probably that go through a lifetime and do what they really love to do. You know and I have had that happen to me in this life, and I’m very grateful for that, yeah. You mentioned the 50s, and your family, and playing Ray Conniff, and I was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts in 1916, and I would say I was © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

exposed to music, you know, from my mom and dad as a child. And see I have recollections of five and six you know, musical recollections. And so what are we talking about? Well ‘56 I did my first album, for Columbia Records. So we’re talking about 40 years, right in the middle of the whole thing, when you started hearing it. People thought in 1956, when my first album came out, like they think about everybody that becomes popular. “Wow, overnight guy here, where’s he been?” But as you think about it there have been 40 years of exposure to music, and my dad played piano, a little piano — he used to play mostly ump-chink chords and sing me little humorous songs you know, and that tickled the heck out of me. But, those little ump-chink chords instilled a rhythm into me, and made me very conscious of rhythm. And then he also played trombone. When I got a little older he taught me to play the trombone when I was about nine. And my mom played piano and used to sing songs to me. So I was exposed to music. I’m 81 now, so I was exposed to music about 40 years when you first heard about me.
The songs that they were playing for you, they were probably considered popular music of that day, were they mostly vocal songs that they had, that you would sing along to?

You know that’s a very interesting question because as I think about it, the music that I used to hear them play and sing, I can remember one, there was one thing that my mother would play, and she would sing like a little soprano lead and my dad would sing like a little obbligato tenor part. And I can’t remember what the piece was, but it was some semi-classical piece, and they used to do that sort of thing. But then you know sometimes people will come up to me like now, in this period of time that we’re doing this interview, I’ll do an interview and someone will say like, “don’t you think some of the music today is really dumb?” You know, and I remember one night they came home and they used to have minstrel shows in those days. And one night they came home from a minstrel show, and my dad was singing, “yes we have no bananas — we have no bananas today.” You know and I mean how dumb can a song be? And so it’s always been that way. There’s been great music and then there’s been very, like frivolous music you know, and then there’s been junk, like that isn’t even music, like rap is that music you know?
No.
It’s rhythm with some story and rhymes and stuff. And music hasn’t changed a lot from what I used to be exposed to.

I think you said a very important thing when you talked about how the ump-chick of your father playing instilled that rhythm in you. Because you can hear that in your arrangements. Do you think that’s one of the keys to what’s made your arranging so successful? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Well you know, you ask very good questions by the way. Up to that point that you’re talking about, when you started hearing my music, I wasn’t before that, prior to that, like when I went through the quote big band era, where I played with the bands like the first big band I played with was Bunny Berigan in 1938. I played trombone and arranged music as well for the band. Then I did the same thing with the Bob Crosby band in 1939, and then I went with the Artie Shaw band in 1940. And now from ‘40 through ‘45 I think I played with three different Artie Shaw bands, and wrote arrangements and played trombone, beside such greats as Jack Jenney and Vernon Brown were in the band. But anyway, during that era — and then I wrote for the Harry James band in 1946. That whole period, and up to where you pointed out when the first album of my own came out, I wrote with a different objective in mind. To me, it was fun and it was a big kick if I wrote a chart as we call them, and I brought it in to the band and they rehearsed it — Jack Jenney or Georgie Auld or Bunny Berigan band or Joe Bushkin in the Bunny Berigan band, or Buddy Rich was in the Bunny Berigan first band I was in. They said, “hey that was a great arrangement, Ray, I like that thing you did on ‘Little Gate.’” I said, “Oh, thanks.” “Little Gate” was the band boy’s name. You know, we never thought, who’s going to know who “Little Gate” is you know? We didn’t think commercially. We just thought, I just thought I wonder how the guys are going to like it. I wrote for the guys. I wrote for Bunny, I wrote for the guys. I wrote for Bob Crosby and the guys in the band. I wrote for Artie Shaw and the guys in the band. I never thought about the people out there that were paying our bills, you know that were paying our salaries, that went to the dances, that listened to us on the air, that bought our records. You know, I didn’t care, I never gave them a second thought. I went through a period I call the lean years, and that was gee, I can’t pin it down, I know I’d been writing for the Harry James Band, ‘46 — I remember the first thing I did for Harry I still had my soldier suit on, I wrote a thing called “Easy,” an original. And Harry and I had a parting of the ways because a few years down the road, I was doing an awful lot of writing for Harry, I wrote a lot of originals for him. And I remember I went into, he had a song for me to do and the name of the song was “Ruby.” And he said, “By the way, why don’t you write a little bit, kind of a bop treatment on this?” Bop was kind of a new school of music that was coming along, and I never did dig bop. I liked to listen to it and I think we had some great players like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. But it was not my bag you know? I like to hear the rhythm, the driving four-four, as Zeke Zarchy always called it, “the driving four-four of the northern American Negro.” And I always liked to hear that, like Buddy Rich played that kind of drums you know. And oh let’s see if I can think of anyone else, I can’t think of any drummers, oh who was the great drummer that was the Shaw bands, one of the first bands I was with — Davey Tough you know. That’s the way I liked to hear the drums. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

And bop was kind of supposed to be a floating type of rhythm on top cymbals and stuff. You weren’t supposed to hear it, you were supposed to feel it here. You were supposed to feel what he was trying — and I don’t know, I never felt that, so I said, “Hey you know, Harry, I just don’t feel that kind of music,” and you know, “maybe it’s time you got another boy.” And his jaw dropped. He looked at me and he couldn’t believe what I was saying. And he said, “well, okay.” So I left the band. For two years I thought all I had to do was pick up the phone and call my old pals, you know, like Sonny Burke at Decca and Paul Weston was at Columbia Records. And I called all of them and told them, “hey I’m free now, I’m not writing steady all the time for Harry, I’m available.” And boy, for two years the phone hardly rang. And finally after sitting waiting for the phone to ring for two years I got so discouraged I thought — I had a wife and a mother I was supporting, and three children, and we were living out in Reseda, and I thought, I’ve got to go get a job. I can’t go on like this. I took a job — they were converting a ten acre, it was a melon field, into a subdivision out in Reseda. And I went out and took a job as a laborer, cleaning up the ditches behind the ditch digger. Where he’d make mistakes on the corner, I’d clean the ditches. And I got to thinking, wow, what happened? Which way did they go, you know. I was making, in 1940, Artie was paying me $300 a week, you know, which in those days was a lot of money. And here I am out digging ditches, you know, for $60 a week. But it gave me a lot of time to think. But anyway I took an awful long — I’ve got to start pinning my answers down, it took a long time to answer your question — but I started thinking completely different about writing arrangements. I thought, what if I started writing for the people that paid the bills, the people that listened, the people that bought the records you know. And I started thinking more along the lines of commercially, and I thought about, you know everything in life is rhythm. Our heartbeat is a rhythm, each day is a rhythm, the sun rises and sets to a rhythm, and the ocean tides go in and out to a rhythm, the cycles of the seasons are a rhythm. And I thought rhythm is very important in our life, and I made the rhythm very predominant. And then I remembered when I first started thinking about the opposite sex. There was a little girl down the street that I had a terrible crush on. I must have been I don’t know, ten, eleven, twelve, something like that. And she was always singing a song, it was [sings], “ooooh, would you like to take a walk — ooooh, do you think it’s going to rain — and something’s gonna come from that” is the name of the song. And to this day, I’ve heard that song once in a while, people will play an old record or a disc jockey. It still moves something. I thought, if I can catch the songs that people fell in love to the first few times, I’ve got a wonderful idea. And that’s what I did. I went back and I thought, when I got my first chance to do an album in 1956, a “wonderful” album, which you heard, or something like it, “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful Nice,” there were three of © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

them — I picked songs, and by arithmetic I went back the number of years, the age group I was trying to hit was 18-35 in the market. So I went back, when were those 18 to 35 year olds hearing, “ooooh would you like to take a walk” with the little girl down the street, or the boy you know, and so by arithmetic I picked songs from the top ten of those years. And that’s what “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful Nice.” So in other words I didn’t change my style of writing that much. I still wrote for brass and saxes, big band style, with a predominant rhythm sound, and I added the voices quite accidentally. It was just an experiment on a single I originally was backing for Columbia Records. And Mitch Miller was head of all the artists at Columbia. He came running out and he says, “this is a great sound. We’ve got to get you back in the studio, have you do a couple of sides, Ray Conniff, orchestra and chorus, and use that orchestra and chorus sound.” And so the first thing we did was a single. It was called on one side was “Begin the Beguine,” and I did some more research and found out that the two songs that had sold the most records, had the most sheet music, and playing, the most airplay and it was “Begin the Beguine” and “Stardust.” That was in 1956. And we put the single out. And it became like a turntable hit. It was played day and night by disc jockeys all over the United States. And as a matter of fact, well no it wasn’t until the album — the single, oddly enough, wasn’t selling very much, with saturation airplay. And Columbia Records would have meetings in the marketing. “What is it with this Conniff? We’re not selling his single and that’s all you hear on the air.” And a fellow by the name of Hal Cook in marketing come up with the answer. He says “you know, I think we’re on the wrong track with Ray Conniff. He’s not a single artist. He’s an album artist. Get him back in the studio with ten more songs and put out an album, and I think we’ll have something.” And so that’s what we did. And one of the other ten songs was “S’ Wonderful,” which we decided to use for the title song, and I used that instruments and — voices and instrument sound and the predominant rhythm sound, and the idea about people falling in love to the songs, and then that album, and the title song of that, “S’ Wonderful,” that became a turntable hit. It was on a chart that Billboard magazine had for about, I don’t know, it’s not on any longer, but it was only ten albums would appear on that chart, and the chart said, “albums most played by disc jockeys” and it was on that list of ten for about nine or ten months. It would be on at five and it would go to seven or eight, it would go back, it would go to two or three, it would go back to nine, and I’d think well that’s it, then it would go back to four, and back to six. It stayed on there for nine or ten months with airplay. But it really didn’t sell quite a bit until about six months. I mean it was negligible — fairly good sales, but after six months it was like your mom and dad or whoever were buying the records in those days, thought okay, somebody says, you can go buy it now if you want. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
They’d heard it so much, the airplay was wonderful. Finally they started going in and it became a gold record. And then we started following it up with a lot of others like it.

That’s so interesting, that I mean it was very astute of you to really have that time off and spend that time digging ditches and really thinking about, now what am I going to do now, and really think about what people wanted to hear and songs they fell in love with, so that you were bringing the business and the music together. Where too often sometimes the businessmen don’t really know music at all. And you pulled them right together.

Yeah, they knew what I was doing too, and they liked the idea too of what I was doing. As a matter of fact I went to a place, a company called Institute of Motivational Research. They got very much interested in the project, and without charging me, they did some research on my product, and then Columbia Records got them into it and we did it further. But you know what was fun about it though, was I didn’t go all the way down the line and do like, you know Guy Lombardo commercial style, or — I can’t think of any other real commercial bands of that time. But I was doing like a big band sound with voices, and I was using the guys that were playing all those things out on the road in the days I was on the road. Like Billy Butterfield was playing lead trumpet, Lou McGarity was playing lead trombone, Panama Francis was in the rhythm section, Dick Hyman was playing piano, and if I couldn’t get Dick I’d get Johnny Guarnieri. And the guys that played with Benny’s band, Hymie Schertzer and Toots Mondello were playing the alto saxophone, Georgie Auld was playing tenor, Jerry Jerome was playing tenor you know. It was an all-star band playing written arrangements by a guy that used to write for the big bands, but was now writing big band style for the people. And the people dug it. They could understand it, you know, because they could hear the melody, even when the guys would play solos, they’d kind of hang around the melody because they knew what I was trying to do you know. I used to write the solos out, and they stayed pretty close to them. And so it was fun to have hit records and be doing something we all enjoyed doing as well.
Let me play something for you here.
Okay.
And talking about your arranging.
Would it be all right if I used one of these?
Sure.
[audio interlude]
Does that ring a bell with you?
Yeah, that’s originally Artie Shaw, isn’t it?
Yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Yeah. In 1940 we recorded that, yeah.
So at this point, you were still writing for the guys in the band, but it still had that very predominant rhythm thing happening, right up front.

Well it’s strange that you picked that particular recording out, because on that particular recording, you know, all through the years working with the bands, and I really started playing I guess, you play professionally when you get paid for a gig. And the first time I got paid for a gig it was in 1933 when I was in high school. And so all through the years, and I was writing at the same time. I must tell you sometime during the interview how I started writing. I got a little device called a “lightning arranger.” I paid a dollar for a mail order device and I wrote my first arrangement with a dollar mail order device. But anyway, you write yourself, don’t you? Yeah. Well you probably, I don’t know if you’re anything like me, I think out of every hundred arrangements I probably write, there’s one that I think really came off either recording or the way I wrote or everything. And this was one when I brought this in and heard this, and heard it performed, I thought, this is one of the best things I’ve ever done for coming together you know, for the whole, the routine, the whole thing. And I thought if I ever get my own group, I’m going to re- record that again. And I would say there were two that I did like that during my whole career with the big bands. The other one was Harry James’ “September Song.” That turned out great too. And both of those arrangements, you know I was trying to give it, as you probably do, all my best effort, you know, my best shot, and work a long time before I put any notes down. But those two really turned out. So I did re-record both of those. So you picked one that even though it was written with the older era of the guys in the band and Artie Shaw, the thought that went into it turned out, although it didn’t use the hit formula idea, the way all the elements came together was, I would say, even though it’s with a great jazz band, it’s commercial you know. People can understand it. They can hear the melody, they can feel the rhythm.
And they were still dancing to the music at that time.
Yeah.
And so it had that kind of — it was a touch of Latin beat in there too.

Yeah I think I always had that. I remember one of the early people that do interviews asked me, “what are the highlights that you think about,” you know in your whole life of music. And one of them, I mentioned that I was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts. And in our house, there was a basement. My dad practically built the house with his own hands. There was a basement, a first floor which had a kitchen, a front hall, living room and dining room, and then the second floor had the bedrooms and a bathroom, and then above, what we used to call the attic. And that was where you kept all the junk you know, the extra stuff. One day I went up in the attic and I discovered a Victrola we called it. It © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

was an old Edison cylinder type Victrola. And there were some of the old records there. And I discovered first, my first initiation into music really, except for what I told you about my mom and dad playing, was to hear the Borodin “Peasant Overture.” And that was a real charge to me. I couldn’t believe things could be like that musically. And I sat and must have listened to that thing for two hours. And then I started looking at some of the other things and there was a lot of Latin stuff there. And I listened to a lot of Latin stuff, and I think I got a feel for Latin very early on from that. And that stuck with me.
And plus your records now, over the years, have been very popular in those countries, in addition to here.

Yeah. One period of time, after quite a few years with the label that I originally went with, I got a call from the Latin division and they said they were getting a lot of calls from South American countries who wanted Ray Conniff to do an album of just Latin music. And so I did my first Latin album, it was called something Latino — Simply Latino [“Latinisimo”], was that it? I can’t remember. But anyway after that it became very successful in South America, and I did quite a few after that, beamed right out to Latin countries only.
Do you think it helped also that your vocals were using — they weren’t singing the lyrics so that there was no language thing there?

Oh yeah. You hit on something that I usually bring out in an interview when I talk about that first album, and they usually say, “what do you think made your albums successful?” And I think that was one of the things. I didn’t have any language barrier. And when Columbia Records sent samples out all over the world, that original “S’ Wonderful” album was picked up all over the world and became quite popular all over the world, as did a lot of the follow up albums. And that was one of the things. Doing the great songs of like Cole Porter, George Gershwin and Jerome Kern, and I had a vocal sound in there with the chorus, but usually when record companies of the U.S.A., which were very big you know, would send samples out to other countries of singers singing these songs of Cole Porter and Gershwin and so forth, they would be in English and there would be a language barrier. And here Ray Conniff comes out with these great songs, with no language barrier, but they still had the voice in there, and they liked that. And so those records became popular all over the world. And you know that I think together with the choice of the material, and the rhythm sound, the voices with instruments and no language barrier, and the idea of picking the hits that people would connect with when they first fell in love, I think that was kind of a three point formula that made it successful all over the world and kept it successful.
Did you start to hear some imitators? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Oh yeah, there were a lot of them. As a matter of fact I wasted about two years of my life trying to find a way to stop them from doing it. And I had attorneys and copyright attorneys and regular attorneys, and we did a lot of research. We found out, they found out that I couldn’t — it’s different now, you can copyright arrangements now — well you could in those days but it was a very complicated thing I ran into. I finally found that the best thing for me to do was to forget about all the imitators, and just keep going on ahead and move ahead, and what came to me, and not worry about if someone else is imitating me. And I found out that they all fell by the wayside, it wasn’t really a — there was only one that really survived and he didn’t survive by copying. There was a fellow in Europe that became quite popular and he originally copied me when he started, but eventually he developed his own style and became — James Last — he became quite well known in Europe.

It seems that the instrumental sound at that time — let me rephrase that — we don’t hear as many instrumental hits anymore you know. You had your music and every once in a while something would come up like “A Walk in the Black Forest,” by Horst Jankowski I think his name was, and then of course the Tijuana Brass. And that it was still possible to have instrumental music be big sellers. I don’t know where that fell by the wayside. I don’t think we hear that that much anymore, just purely instrumental music, unless it’s Kenny G I guess he’s a name we know.
Yeah. The last one I can really thing of [scats].
“The Hustle,” yeah.
That was a big hit. What was his name? I can’t think of his name.
Do the hustle.

Yeah you’re right. Like in the old days, the big bands had a lot of instrumental hits, “In the Mood,” and “String of Pearls” and those kind of things. But you know I think probably even in the old days, for every instrumental hit, weren’t there three or four vocal hits? With lyrics? I think instrumental hits have never been the big thing, but I don’t think it’s changed a lot but it is true. I think in my own case, in Latin countries I’ve had a lot of instrumental hits, like “Besame Mucho” was a tremendous hit, my arrangement of that was a big hit in Latin America. When we do tours down there, we include several songs, there’s “Besame Mucho” — when I play that they’ll all start singing the arrangement. And “Green Eyes” was another one down there. “Beyond the Sea” was a big hit down there, “Brazil” was a big hit. “Night and Day.” There was an album I did down there it was called “A Touch of Latin” and it had all of those songs in it. And we almost have to include those when we do tours or they’ll ask for them from the audience. And so that would be the exception with me. I’ve had a lot of instrumental hits down there.
I want to go back to this music chord transposer, this device. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Oh it was called a “lightning arranger.” Yeah. That was about 1934, I was a junior in high school, or no, I was a senior by then. And I was playing with this little band. We were playing stocks you know. And we had trumpet, trombone — well we never could get a good second trumpet. We usually had trumpet and trombone and sometimes if we had a bigger gig we’d have three brass. And three saxes and drums and piano. And we could never get a good bass player. And we’d play stocks. But anyway we played for the school dances you know. And one day I was looking for something in my dad’s room. And he was secretary of the musicians’ union in Attleboro, Massachusetts, played trombone in the marching band you know, and took care of their business for them. And I was looking for something in the desk and he subscribed to Billboard magazine. And I started thumbing through it. And down in the lower right corner, I remember it was the right hand page, was a little box about, I don’t know, a couple inches, less than a couple of inches high, it said “Lightning Arranger.” I can’t remember the wording, but learn to arrange overnight, you know, instantaneous arranging. What it was, it was a transposing device. And in this way — is it okay if I write, oh I don’t have a pencil, yeah I think I have something. It was — we used to call it celluloid. Is it okay if I write on here? Now we call it plastic. But it was about, let me see I’ll get this up to the camera after, okay, and I’ll give you an idea. Because it’s easy to understand if you see this. There was, okay, I won’t go this whole, but I’ll show you how one of the wheels would look. Okay. Now there were two plastic pieces, and you know picture one of these and then another one. And in between there was a wheel in here, see? And you could turn the wheels here. Then there were slots. I didn’t put all the slots in. And you could turn it over and there were more slots see, on the back. So here would say like it would say concert instruments, like piano. It would give a C chord. You’d have a C, a G, E and a C. The C chord. Then here it would say B flat trumpets. And it would say D, A, F sharp, D. Then here would say E flat saxophones, which would be what A, E, C sharp A you know. And so you had the C chord here, and if you wanted to write for with what I play trumpet, we had a trumpet, E flats, and we had tenor saxophone, which also comes under the heading of the trumpets, you know, the B flat trumpet. So I could write a C chord for those four instruments, and know what notes to write for them. And then over on this side here, on these slots over here, this would say C7.
Okay, we’ve got the dominant chords coming.

And this would be for C7, and then there would be slots that say ninths. Here would say diminished, augmented, and you’d turn over and you’d have the whole ball of wax. So I thought this was great. So I took the ninth thing and I put it down and I just happened to have it on F7 see? So I played the F7, no I had it on F9, no I had an F7. So I played the F7, and I turned the wheel, and I just accidentally turned it in the direction of the cycle of © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

the fifths. And the next slot was B flat 7. So I struck the B flat 7 and held the thing down. I turned it another notch and hit the E flat 7. Wow. That’s “Sweet Georgia Brown,” you know? And so I wrote my first arrangement, and I turned it over and I did, instead of F7 I did the ninth chords. And I did “Sweet Georgia Brown,” for trumpet, trombone and three saxes. And I used the five way, no double lead you know. And it was like Duke was writing in those days. And I brought that into the guys and they fell on the floor [scats]. And you know with just five ways — imagine what that sound — nobody had ever heard anything like that. You know they weren’t writing like that then.
That’s a great story.
So for one dollar —
How long did you hold on to that thing?

Oh boy do I wish I had that today, yeah. For one dollar, what an investment. And of course I used it for a while as a transposing device, but that led me into writing, because later on I studied and I would, I started with Hugo Friedhofer, by the way, boy he was great. Do you remember him? He wrote for the motion pictures out here on the west coast. And then I ran into, who was it, somebody tipped me off to start looking into the classics, and I started taking Tchaikovsky’s scores — did you ever do that? You take like “Romeo and Juliet” and you put it down, everything down into concert so you can look at it quicker. I re-scored it down into concert, and the simplicity of Tchaikovsky’s writing was amazing when you saw it that way. And also that’s where I started learning the beauty of — I think that’s one thing that’s a little missing today. Did you by the way see — who’s the great fellow, the interviewer, the top interviewer on CNN, what’s his name?
Not Ted Koppel.

No, no, no, no. Larry King. He had Eric Clapton on. And he was playing guitar, and I think except the way I heard him and his writings with the guitar, mainly today, well a point I want to make is a lot of today’s music is being written by guitar players. You can’t — with the guitar you miss the beauty of a Tchaikovsky, like [scats], you know the third in the bass. The seventh and the bass. With a guitar you always have the tonic in the bass. And I think that’s missing a little bit in the younger writers today. They write with the guitar. They need to study those classics and see the beauty, the great sound of a third in the bass and not doubled in the harmony. You know, leave the third out in the harmony. It’s only down there. There’s something about that, it just moves me, I don’t know.

It’s interesting you mention that, because if you look at — recently I was looking at some of the music from “West Side Story,” and “One Hand One Heart.” And that’s what Bernstein did. He had very simple chords, but he would put the third in the bass, and it changed the whole thing, it gave it a real beautiful effect. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

Well if you took Tchaikovsky and put the melody in the bass line, you’ve practically got a composition and a score like this you know. But with today’s writers, everything’s going like this. But there’s something about that contrary motion and the movement of the bass, it’s great. But I learned that from breaking those scores down, you know, and I thought wow, what a sound, that’s great, that’s how they do that, huh? And I’d hunt, and wait a minute now, have an F chord and there would be an A in the bass, and I’d be looking, it must be, he’s got guys way up in there, he must have an A somewhere there. And I’d look at it — no A. No A. It’s only down in the bass.

That’s an important lesson too, in that I know that I’ve thought sometimes when I’ve been trying to orchestrate something and I don’t have enough notes, and gee, this guy’s got nothing to play. And you’re tempted, instead of giving him a rest, to give that person a note to play. But maybe it’s not really necessary.

Oh you know, that’s a great lesson. I learned that from Hugo — I learned it, he taught me, but I don’t use it all the time, he’d say, “Ray, one of the things that you can learn, the fewer guys you use to get the desired result, and the fewer notes you use to get the desired result that you’re after, it’s always going to sound better.” And that’s a hard one. You’ve got 60 guys there, you want everybody playing all the time, you know, especially the producer, wants everybody playing all the time — “we’re paying them aren’t we?” And sometimes you have only one-third or one-tenth of them playing, and then bring them in, and then let it come out, and then let it go back down to just a few guys you know. We don’t talk like this all the time do we? We have nuances when we talk. We talk like this, we emphasize things, and de-emphasize things. And music has to be the same way.

Let me ask you a kind of a business question. As you became a well known arranger and producer and so forth, were you able to get better business arrangements with your record company? Did you kind of hold more power in the structure of things?

Well you must have had an arrangement like with Columbia, did you get a percentage of the recording? Were you on contract?

Oh I started out like all the rest of the artists. The first break I got was through Mitch Miller. I met Mitch when I was writing for Harry James’ band, and he would come out to the west coast, and sit in the booth and oversee the sessions. And when I first went back to New York, this is let’s say five or six years later, after I’d been doing arranging for Harry James, I went back — I’d been on the west coast for a while and I decided gee I used to do, I was doing well, but I thought I could be doing better. It seemed like I’m not quite fulfilling what I could really do. And I came in as a trombonist on a record session and Mitch was in the booth on the session. And he came out and said, “hey, Ray, what © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

you doing in New York?” And I said, “well I’m in town now,” and you know we used to talk about my ideas that I was telling you about, writing commercially for the people about when they fell in love and the time period and the predominance of the rhythm. I said, “you know if you need any arranging done, I’m here, available now,” and he says, “fine, I’ll keep you in mind“ the old line you know — don’t call us we’ll call you. And I thought oh the same old thing. But sure enough, two weeks later he called me, and he got me in to do backings for a girl called Eileen Rogers. And by the way, while I was out in California, during the lean years, I forgot to tell you about this, you know I told you about the lean years? I went out and at the suggestion of Frank DeVol, I bought a book called The Grammar of Conducting. Did you ever see that book? You buy yourself a mirror and you put it up on the wall and you get the music stand, and you picture the full orchestra, all 60 of them, and you conduct “Romeo and Juliet” and you cue everything you know, and you do the whole thing, and you learn you don’t conduct like this. And you keep time, this is a one, and most guys that don’t do it, they just lead like this all the time. But anyway so I studied The Grammar of Conducting, and I started taking piano lessons, which I never did overcome, I never became accomplished on the keyboard. And I would practice the trombone, and I would write. And so anyway, so now it’s coming together. So he called me in about an Eileen Rogers, two sides. And he said to me at the close of the interview, she was there, I got her key you know. And he said as I’m going out the door he said, “by the way, why don’t you write yourself a couple of trombone parts if you want to make yourself a couple extra bucks.” And as I tell you this story, what I’m going to tell you now, took place in about ten seconds. It takes a long time to tell it, but it took place back and forth, a little exchange. The first exchange was, “why don’t you write yourself a couple of trombone parts if you want to make yourself a couple of extra bucks.” And I says, “well who’s conducting?” And this, if you knew me in those days, I’m such an introvert. For me to ask a question like this, God must have been looking over me. I don’t know how I ever asked that question. And he said, “well I’ve got a conductor.” It was a split session. You know how they’d put four songs in on a side, and one artist would do two songs, and another would do two songs. Don Cherry was doing two songs, and Eileen Rogers, my artist was doing two songs. So what he’s telling me is, “I’ve got a conductor hired, Norm Layton is going to be conducting” for Don Cherry, you know, it’s a split session. And I asked the question. So this is the way it went. So he says, “Write yourself a couple of trombone parts.” “Well who’s going to conduct?” And he said, “why would you like to conduct?” And I said, “well yeah.” He said okay. That’s how long it took for me to become a conductor. A complete introvert, that always would say oh, okay, okay you’ve © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

got a conductor, I’ll bring the arrangements in and give them to him. So this was the first time. He thought this is great. This guy is great. So he started giving me all his artists. I did Don Cherry’s “Band of Gold,” do you remember that a little later? And her little body, she was very small then, her little body was just shaking she was so nervous. I says, “Rosie, you’re Rosie Clooney, aren’t you?” And she says, “Yeah.” I says, “You are great, what are you worried about? You are such a great success.” She is one of the greatest musicians I’ve ever worked with. And she sang a note, bing, it was right on the button. I mean she didn’t scoop up to the note, she really hit them right in tune and stayed in tune, and a great sound. So she was wonderful. So she relaxed and she sang great. anyway, so we did the Rosie sessions, and you asked — I still didn’t answer the question about the deal. would come out. I never worried about what was in the contract. So it finally got up where I got — I was what they called in those days a flat artist. No kidding.

Now, musicians and singers, and I’m really, I go in with a time schedule and a budget. You know, I know what I’m doing. Three percent of nothing isn’t very good.
Yeah, right.

I’ve noticed that at that time you had a timeframe that you had to work in, or that you chose to work in, for each song, that as I look at these titles, the longest cut I see is like three minutes and fifteen seconds. Was that mostly for a radio consideration or was it just for the listeners’ attention span?

Well there were two things that went into that. The radio was a very big part of it, airplay. If you had a song that was 3:15 and someone else had a song that was 2:15, and the guy’s making up his show, he would pick the 2:15 unless he really wanted to play, you know, because he wanted to get more commercials in. And we were all kind of keeping our cuts down as much as we could, because we got a better chance of airplay on the cuts if they were around 2:15 — 2:20 was ideal. To go under it you were getting, the buyer wasn’t getting enough music, and you didn’t really have a chance to get a good idea in the arrangements. The other thing was that on the album sides, long cuts — well let’s see — we were putting out twelve songs to an album originally, six on a side. And they © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
eventually cut that to five on a side because of the royalties and the payments for the songs you know. Let’s see you asked about the timing.

So if you write your arrangement then, you had to actually figure out what’s the tempo of this song, and kind of time like how many choruses can I do, should I go to the bridge here sooner than I was going to. You had to keep in mind the time as you put the structure of the song together.

Yeah. Like you’ll have a watch — this is a second hand and like if I was here and I got a great idea and I said, “do you mind if we stop the tape a minute” I can sing myself eight bars and stop it, and say okay let’s go on, and I can go home and I can remember the song and what the tempo was by the eight bars. Yeah I would time everything out, and would shoot for around — well I didn’t make it a real rule, you know, because you always had some songs in there that you put in there for airplay. I remember on the album of “Broadway and Rhythms,” “On the Street Where you Live” was almost 2:10, something about like 2:10, and I got a lot of airplay on that. So that was the cut in that album. I knew the guys would play that cut out of the album, because everybody liked that. So I didn’t worry too much, maybe another one could be up around three. Another thing, I wonder if the people that might hear this might be interested in knowing, we don’t have an album in here, but in the middle of this album, when you’re playing an album, when the needle’s out here, the revolutions of the record player in those days is always the same, 33-1/3 revolutions per minute. So when the needle is out here, it’s going around this big long circumference. When it’s in here, it’s going a very short distance in the same period of time. The quality is much poorer here. The quality is three times as good out here as it is here. And we had to think about that, in the timing of the album, how far apart the grooves were, and how far we would go in here. Because you’d get to a certain point here, and the quality got so poor in there that you didn’t want to use it anymore.
I never thought of that.
We don’t have that problem with CDs and numbers and digital and all of that.
Yeah. And it relates to tape speed too. When if you tape something—

No tape speed is determined what’s going across the heads. It’s pulled through the heads by the rollers. Well actually the reel is going faster or slower, but the speed of the tape through the heads is always the same.
Oh. Okay.
15 IPS we used to record, and now we double it.
Did that idea of the songs that are in the middle of the record, might not sound quite as good, did that determine what arrangements you might put in there?

Not so much as the first band would determine. You figure when a disc jockey got a new album, or they used to let people go in the record stores and play and listen, you figured © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

people were going to listen to the first band and maybe skip to the second. We always thought those were the most important bands. That if they liked the first couple of bands they’d buy the album or they’d put it on the air. So those were the ones. We didn’t pay too much attention to the inner bands because we knew the quality wasn’t as good anyway.
Wow. I never thought of that.
I don’t know if other artists — maybe other artists never thought of those things. But I was very commercial and looked at all aspects of the business. I got into the covers and everything.

Yeah, talking about the process of recording music, I mean you’ve seen from your days with Bunny Berigan up until your most recent one hundredth album, which I wanted to mention, you’ve seen a great deal of change in the actual technology of recording. Do you think it’s affected the music in the way it’s written, the way that technology has changed the recording of it?

It has in this way, that well let’s see, it’s hard to answer that. You know I think overdubbing has changed things a little bit. Because I remember as long as I’ve been in this business you’re always learning new things. The very last album I did was this one here called “I Love Movies” which is a very new album. It just reached the market, and it’s movie themes, stuff like “Star Wars,” John Williams — I have two John Williams in, he’s great, I love John Williams, “Star Wars” and “Can You Read My Mind,” — talk about, you know, melody and bass line, now you’re talking about a musician you know. And all of kind of today’s movie themes. I was recording and I was going to overdub the singers on “Can You Read My Mind,” which had lyrics. Usually if I have lyrics — by the way, I do everything simultaneously. I’m going back, I went through — in the beginning I recorded everything simultaneously in the studio, and then I tried a period of time where I went to the overdubbing technique by going in, record the rhythm section you know, and then I’d bring the brass and then saxes or the brass in and record to the rhythm, or bring the saxes in and record to the brass and the rhythm, and then bring the singers in and add them on top of everything. And this — we’re going to get into a technical thing now, but we’re getting into something that really improves the quality of each section in that you don’t have the sound of the drums, like in the first recordings we did, I’m going back now into ‘56, the one you first heard. You don’t have the drums. When the drum catches a punctuation by the brass, he leaks into some of the other mics, which changes the drum sound, which changes things around. But leakage is not that bad. But when you do the rhythm tracks alone and you put the drummer in a booth by himself, all you hear on the drum tracks is the drum, no leakage. So in other words, you don’t get drums leaking into singers, like we used to have on “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

Nice.” You don’t get brass leaking into singers, like we have on “S’ Wonderful.” You don’t get brass leaking into piano, and drums leaking into piano. And you get clean tracks on everybody. But you do lose something I think. You lose the idea of 28 people in the studio at the same time recording a piece of music and hearing what everybody else is doing, and how the finished product is sounding. With the brass overdubbing technique, you do your rhythm tracks and the drummers are hearing the guitars on earphones. The guitars aren’t next to him. He’s not feeling them the same. And when the brass come in to overdub to the rhythm, they’re wearing earphones. He’s not really hearing the trumpets next to him as much as he did — well he has one ear and he does hear out of here, he hears the other trumpet, but it’s a whole different ball game. And one has advantages and disadvantages, and the other has advantages and disadvantages. I prefer everybody live in the studio at the same time. If you need a little more singers on something that had words, overdub them. And you have a feeling of excitement and fun that is on the record that doesn’t get there by the overdubbing technique. Now let’s see, what got us into this — you asked about changes—
In the recording process.

Well that’s why I thought we should mention overdubbing, because I think that changes it a bit. It changes the writing a bit when you think you’re writing for overdubbing and not for something else, you know not for live. I think basically the answer would be no, wouldn’t it? That you wouldn’t change a lot because of the techniques.

Oh I was just talking about I guess the sound of your recordings and the technology. Yeah, it happens. Like the syn drums, remember the syn drums? I used those for a while and then I stopped using them because they were being used so much. I think that on the whole things have gone forward recording-wise. I’m using synthesizers now. I used them on this last album, CD. I don’t use them quite the same as the younger artists use them. Girls with double unisons with trumpets and higher saxophones. And I tried, hey I think I’ll embellish that, let’s try going a little further, let’s use a synthesizer with it as well. It’s too hard. It could be done if they did that for a living, you know. But anyway this fellow that is head of Polygram, the international department, was with SONY Music and he came to a concert, came backstage, “Ray, why don’t you come on Polygram.” He says, “how are things going with SONY?” I says, “oh they take me for granted after 40 years, they don’t promote.” He says, “come with me, I’ll promote you.” So he’s been doing, he sent this kit out. So anyway, when we first met about what I should do, which answers your question, I said, “well what do you think we should do for a first album?” And he came up with the “I Love Movies” idea, you know with the heart for the love. And he said, “I’m going to send you a cassette of not ten — we were going to put ten songs originally, it wound up twelve. He said, “I’ll send you not ten, but I want to send you about 30 songs of movie themes, because he says, I want you to go through them.” And he says, “what I’ve noticed about when Ray Conniff does an arrangement of a song, it kind of becomes your song in a way, because it’s different than it was any other time anyone else did it.” He says, “I want you to listen to 30, and pick ten that you can make your sound on.” And that’s the way I did it. So I took the 30 and went through all 30, and I listened to each one quite a bit. And I will first work with the sheet music and first I’ll listen to the theme as it was done in the movie, like the “Star Wars” theme by John Williams, or “Can You Read © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

My Mind.” And then I will get the sheet music out and sit at the piano and just kind of see what comes to me. And I’ll make notes up on the piano part of ideas that came to me on that. And I went through all 30, and I make kind of pencil notes on the piano bar. Or I might grab a piece of manuscript or something if there wasn’t room to put it on the piano part, and I’ll put “Star Wars” on the outside and scribble out a little line that I have. Like on “Star Wars” what comes to me is that I started fiddling with the chords of “Star Wars,” and I happened to be in G, which “Somewhere My Love” was in. And I’d just come from a rehearsal with the singers and we’d been rehearsing that, and I started playing [scats], which is the same as the piano background of “Somewhere My Love.” I says hey you know what? That would work on this. And I just took the G, D, G, B, G, D, G, D, B, C [scats]. And used the “Somewhere My Love” background piano pattern with “Star Wars.” And [scats] I did a much slower tempo. And used the trombones and men and low saxes for the theme [scats]. And so I’d write that idea down, and go through all 30. Then I’ll go back through and I will think about, I’m leaving it up to him to send me 30 that he says to him it doesn’t make any difference which ten I pick. And I will think though about you know, “Star Wars” had a lot of publicity. You know it had a big push. So if I can fit in with songs that have had — like if now I was doing it I’d certainly have put some stuff from “Titanic” in you know, it’s so big, that people are going to see songs from “Titanic” in the CD and they’re going to lean towards that. So I’ll lean that way a little. But on the whole, I’ll get the best ten ideas and those are the ones that will wind up in the album.

Great. Well I wish you a lot of success with it and I am fascinated by your combination over the years of business sense, with the great musicianship. That’s rare. I think that’s rare. Because I’ve talked to a number of people who bemoan the fact that the people in power in the music world these days seem to have no musical sense or whatever. And so it’s nice to see it.

Well there has been quite a change. When I started I mentioned Mitch Miller who was an oboe player, and Goddard Lieberson who was president of Columbia Records was a graduate of Juilliard. And they were musicians, or if they weren’t musicians they were guys that wished they could have been musicians that were in [coughs] they were musicians or guys that at least wished they could have been musicians. Now in the record companies they are more concentrating on what’s at the bottom line, how much money did we make or lose, and they have accountants and attorneys running the companies. And I liked it better when the musicians were running the companies. I owe a lot to the fellows that gave me my chance you know, to do that, and I owe a lot to disc jockeys too, they played the heck out of my stuff in the beginning, and fellows like you that did interviews and wrote articles on my music too, and in the trade magazine Down © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-

Beat and Record World and Variety and those magazines, Billboard. They really gave me a lot of space. Of course in the final analysis I had owe a lot to the people that I hit that heart string and recorded that song they fell in love to, and they went out and bought the albums. I have to thank all them too. They’ve been great and they’ve stayed with me for years.

Well I think probably there’s a lot of song composers that are very fond of you also, because I’m sure some of them have gotten some royalties out of all the records you’ve sold, because of the great arrangements you’ve written of their music.

It’s been fun because I’ve been able to do what I’ve done all the years through the band days and the big band days and playing trombone — I still play trombone, when I go out on the tours I’ll play a little Jack Teagarden, I’ll play “Basin Street Blues,” or “I’ve Got a Right to Sing the Blues” or something. And I still have great musicians in the band. And it’s fun to play what I call good music, but still done in a way that the people that are out there listening and coming to the concerts can understand and enjoy as well.

Well that sounds like a great way to wrap up. And I want to say on camera that I’m very grateful to you for making the trip down from L.A. also, with the things going on in your life and you’re busy, and I really appreciate your coming down. And I wish you all the best.
Gee I never listened to a sound check. I know on the kit they sent out the sound wasn’t very great, but I hope everything came out all right, but I’ve had a little rasp in my throat.
Well I also noticed on one of, on the tape that they sent that you like to sing along but it’s “off mic” you said.
Oh, yeah, yeah, I have no chops. I don’t have a good sound. Yeah I do sing along with the horns and voices, but I prefer it if they don’t get me too predominant on a mic.
Okay, well it was a great pleasure talking to you.

Thank you very much, Monk, and gee lots of success. I understand you’ve got about a hundred others, interviews like this in there. I hope some day I may get back to see you and may be able to see a little of them.
Please when you come out to view the fall colors in the east, maybe we can have you as a guest.
Okay, well I must take your card and your address along. Are you anywhere near 80 or 70? Route 70 or 80? The big east-west highways? Are you near 40? You’d be up north.
We are on the New York State Thruway, I-90.
90. Yeah. You’d be up, I’d have to go through the northern route to go through your area probably. Okay.
Thanks so much.
All right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-

segments.title: Opening and introduction by Monk Rowe
segments.summary: Rowe introduces Conniff and the 'Ray Conniff sound' and asks if he would do it all again.

segments.title: No regrets; born in Attleboro and early musical exposure
segments.summary: Conniff says he is fortunate to have done what he loves, was born in Attleboro in 1916, and was exposed to music by his parents; his dad taught him trombone at about nine.

segments.title: Parents' songs, minstrel shows and opinions on today's music
segments.summary: The semi-classical duets his parents sang, the 'Yes We Have No Bananas' minstrel show night, and Conniff's view that there has always been great, frivolous and junk music, rap included.

segments.chapter: Big band years and the lean years
segments.title: Big band years writing for the guys: Berigan, Crosby, Shaw, James
segments.summary: Conniff lists his jobs from Berigan in 1938 to Shaw and James in 1946, wrote for the musicians not the public, and recounts the 'Ruby' bop request.

segments.chapter: Big band years and the lean years
segments.title: Quitting Harry James over bop; lean years digging ditches
segments.summary: Conniff tells James he doesn't feel bop and quits, gets no calls for two years, works as a ditch laborer in Reseda, and decides to write for the paying public with strong rhythm.

segments.title: First Columbia album: 'S Wonderful and choosing songs by arithmetic
segments.summary: He picks top-ten hits from the years his 18-35 audience fell in love, adds voices by accident, Mitch Miller likes it, and the 'S Wonderful album becomes a gold record.

segments.title: Market research and the all-star players on the albums
segments.summary: Motivational research helped, and Conniff used former big band sidemen such as Butterfield, McGarity, Hyman and Auld to play written arrangements for the public.

segments.title: Audio clip: Shaw recording and Conniff's best arrangements
segments.summary: After a clip of an Artie Shaw recording from 1940, Conniff names it and Harry James's 'September Song' as his two best arrangements, which he later re-recorded.

segments.title: Attic Victrola and early Latin influences
segments.summary: In the Attleboro house attic he found an Edison Victrola with the Borodin 'Peasant Overture' and Latin records, which gave him an early feel for Latin music.

segments.title: Latin albums for South American audiences
segments.summary: The Latin division asked for an all-Latin album, which succeeded in South America and led to several more.

segments.title: No language barrier and the three-point formula for success
segments.summary: Wordless voices let the albums sell worldwide; he credits choice of material, rhythm, voices with instruments, and hits tied to first love.

segments.title: Imitators and James Last
segments.summary: Conniff wasted two years with attorneys trying to stop imitators before moving on; only James Last survived by developing his own style.

segments.title: Instrumental hits then and now, and Latin America favorites
segments.summary: Discussion of instrumental hits, vocal hits outnumbering them in the big band era, and Conniff's own instrumental hits in Latin America like 'Besame Mucho'.

segments.title: The 'lightning arranger' and first arrangement of 'Sweet Georgia Brown'
segments.summary: A one-dollar mail-order transposing wheel from Billboard led the high school senior to write his first five-part arrangement, astonishing his bandmates.

segments.title: Studying with Hugo Friedhofer and Tchaikovsky scores
segments.summary: The lightning arranger led to study; he started with Hugo Friedhofer and re-scored Tchaikovsky into concert pitch to learn his simplicity.

segments.title: Thirds in the bass and guitar-based writing today
segments.summary: Conniff says many young writers write from guitar and miss the beauty of the third in the bass he learned from Tchaikovsky; Rowe cites Bernstein.

segments.title: Friedhofer's lesson: fewer players and fewer notes
segments.summary: Friedhofer taught that fewer players and notes sound better, and music needs nuance like speech.

segments.title: Mitch Miller gives Conniff his first break
segments.summary: Conniff met Miller during the James years, returned to New York, and got a call to arrange for Eileen Rogers; he also studied conducting during the lean years.

segments.title: First conducting and hit arrangements for Miller's artists
segments.summary: Conniff sets tempos for the first time, then arranges hits for Don Cherry, Johnnie Ray, Johnny Mathis and Marty Robbins with whistle and piano hooks.

segments.title: Working with Rosie Clooney in California
segments.summary: Miller takes Conniff west; only the Rosie Clooney session happens, and he praises her nervous warmth and perfect pitch.

segments.title: The three percent royalty contract
segments.summary: Conniff received 'Begin the Beguine' as a single and signed a stock Columbia contract at three percent of the record price, netting about eighteen cents an album.

segments.title: Flat artist deal, recording costs and top royalty
segments.summary: Mitch Miller raised him to the five percent top royalty; Conniff explains recording budgets then and now and that selling product gets a good deal.

segments.title: Keeping cuts around 2:15 for radio airplay
segments.summary: Radio programmers favored shorter songs, so Conniff timed arrangements carefully, with exceptions such as 'On the Street Where You Live'.

segments.title: LP groove quality and putting strong cuts first
segments.summary: Conniff explains inner grooves sound poorer, so the first bands were most important; tape speed is also touched on.

segments.title: Overdubbing versus recording live in the studio
segments.summary: On recording technology, Conniff discusses leakage, overdubbing and why he prefers all players live together.

segments.title: Billy Butterfield albums and too much reverb
segments.summary: After an audio clip, Conniff says on 'Just Kiddin' Around' with Billy Butterfield he went overboard with reverb.

segments.title: Synthesizers and new technology
segments.summary: Synthesizers failed to phrase like trombones and voices, but a sustained string pad worked well on the new CD.

segments.title: Fan club in Germany
segments.summary: Rowe asks about a fan club; Conniff says there is the Ray Conniff International Fan Club.

segments.title: Moving to Polygram and arranging 'I Love Movies'
segments.summary: After 40 years with Columbia, Conniff signed with Polygram and explains how he picks ten of 30 movie themes and sketches ideas at the piano, as with 'Star Wars'.

segments.title: Musicians versus accountants running record companies
segments.summary: Conniff says Miller and Goddard Lieberson were musicians while today's companies are run by accountants, and he thanks DJs, the press and fans.

segments.title: Still playing trombone on tours
segments.summary: Conniff still plays Jack Teagarden-style trombone on tours and enjoys good music the audience can understand.

segments.title: Closing remarks and goodbyes
segments.summary: Thanks, a sound check worry, singing off mic, and talk of a future visit to Hamilton.
